title: Independent-Samples t-Test: The Null Distribution
summary: The tool works from summary statistics, because that is all a t-test needs, and puts the whole test into one picture: the distribution of t if the two population means were equal, with the tails beyond the observed statistic shaded, the critical values as dashed rules and the standard normal drawn faintly behind so the heavier tails at small degrees of freedom can be seen rather than asserted. Two preset buttons run the same two groups at fifteen and at a hundred per group, so the same finding is read off twice with Cohen's d fixed at 0.50 and p falling from .182 to below .001. A closing challenge asks the learner to choose between four write-ups of one non-significant result.
learningObjectives: Build t from a mean difference and a standard error and place it on the null distribution.
Read a two-tailed p as the area beyond the observed statistic.
Explain why p depends strongly on the sample size while Cohen's d does not.
Explain why the t distribution has heavier tails than the normal and why the gap closes with degrees of freedom.
Write a conclusion that says fail to reject rather than accept, and that reports an interval alongside the decision.
interactionTypes: live null distribution with shaded tails
critical regions that move with alpha
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every value is computed in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, a select, radio groups and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the sample-size slider announces both the size and the degrees of freedom it produces. The chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired inside its figure with a visible four-row table giving the observed statistic, the critical value, the tail area and the decision in words, and a disclosure holds the confidence interval for the mean difference beside the critical values of t and of the normal. The shaded tails carry a vertical hatch as well as a fill, the observed statistic is a labelled rule, the critical values are labelled dashed rules, and the normal curve is dashed, so no part of the reading depends on colour. The decision is always printed as reject or fail to reject, never accept. The pinned primary result measures 514px tall at 1366x768. Every preset and control announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: One number on one curve: where t comes from, and why p moves with n when d does not
simulationNotes: No data are generated: the tool takes two means, two standard deviations and a sample size and computes the pooled standard deviation as the root mean square of the two group SDs, the standard error as the pooled SD times the square root of two over n, t as the mean difference over that standard error on 2n-2 degrees of freedom, Cohen's d as the mean difference over the pooled SD, and the two-tailed p from the regularised incomplete beta function. Critical values are found by bisection on the tail area, which avoids a separate inverse-t routine and also supplies the confidence interval for the mean difference; the interval excludes zero exactly when the test rejects, and the tool says so. The t density and the standard normal density are both drawn, so the heavier tails at small df are visible rather than asserted. The tool warns when the two standard deviations differ by more than a factor of 1.8, because this is the classic pooled-variance test and Welch's version, which does not assume equal variances, is not computed here. Group sizes are equal throughout. The reference figures a lecturer can check: at fifteen per group with means 50 and 55 and SDs of 10, SE = 3.65, t(28) = 1.37, d = 0.50, p = .182, critical value 2.05; at a hundred per group the same two groups give SE = 1.41, t(198) = 3.54, d = 0.50 and p below .001. All studies, groups and scores are fictional.
